```{python}
from pathlib import Path

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
```

# Summary

# Introduction
**Does flipper length or body mass more accurately classify penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap, Gentoo)?**
## Background
The Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2020) contains body measurements of adult Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins (genus *Pygoscelis*) nesting on three islands in Antarctica's Palmer Archipelago: Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen. The data were collected from 2007 to 2009 by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) program, as part of a study of differences between male and female penguins.

Every breeding season, researchers identified studies nests where pairs of adults were present prior to egg-laying and consistently monitored these sites. Once a nest was found to have one egg, both adults were captured, measured, and had a blood sample taken to determine each penguin's sex (Gorman et al., 2014). Consequently, every observation in the data set represents a breeding adult measured at the same point in the nesting cycle. 

## Relevance
Exploring how flipper length and body mass independently relates to penguin species is valuable because the two measurements describe very different kinds of traits. Flipper length is structural: once a penguin is fully grown, it stays roughly constant. In comparison, body mass varies based on factors like foraging success and breeding effort, so it reflects a penguin's current condition as much as its species. Finding out which one better separates the species tells us whether species differences are better captured by stable body structure or by size that fluctuates, which matters for any study that compares penguins measured at different times or under different conditions.

## Data Description
We use the `penguins` data set from the `palmerpenguins` package (Horst et al., 2020), which contains 344 penguins: 152 Adélie, 68 Chinstrap and 124 Gentoo. Each row represents one adult penguin and records its species, island, bill length, bill depth, flipper length, body mass, sex and study year. Our analysis uses three of these variables:

- `species`: penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap or Gentoo); the target we classify.
- `flipper_length_mm`: flipper length, in millimetres.
- `body_mass_g`: body mass, in grams.

Two penguins have no flipper length or body mass recorded, so we remove them before analysis. The remaining variables are not used.

# Methods
## Data Collection

We used the Palmer Penguins dataset, which contains measurements and species information for penguins observed in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. The dataset was obtained from the publicly available GitHub repository maintained by the Palmer Penguins project (Horst et al., 2020).

We focused on three variables: penguin species, flipper length, and body mass. Species was used as the response variable, while flipper length and body mass were evaluated separately as predictors.

```{python}
# Create data directories
raw_dir = Path("../data/raw")
processed_dir = Path("../data/processed")

raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Download the original dataset
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv"
raw_data = pd.read_csv(url)

# Save the original dataset
raw_data.to_csv(raw_dir / "penguins.csv", index=False)

# Select relevant variables and remove missing values
data = raw_data[
    ["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
].dropna()

# Save processed data
data.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_cleaned.csv", index=False)
```

## Traing-Test Splitting
We divided the cleaned dataset into training and testing sets using a 75:25 ratio. 
We performed this split before exploratory data analysis and preprocessing to prevent information from the test set from influencing model development.

```{python}

train_data, test_data = train_test_split(
    data,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=123,
    stratify=data["species"]
)

# Separate response variable and predictors
y_train = train_data["species"]
y_test = test_data["species"]

X_train_flipper = train_data[["flipper_length_mm"]]
X_test_flipper = test_data[["flipper_length_mm"]]

X_train_mass = train_data[["body_mass_g"]]
X_test_mass = test_data[["body_mass_g"]]
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

We explored the training data to understand how flipper length and body mass vary across the three penguin species. 
We calculated descriptive statistics and created boxplots to examine differences between species and identify potential overlap in their measurements.

```{python}
# Descriptive statistics
summary_stats = train_data.groupby("species")[

summary_stats
```

## Model Training
We used logistic regression to classify penguins into three species: Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo with  
Logistic regression is a classification method that estimates the probability of an observation belonging to each class.

To compare the predictive ability of the two measurements, we developed two separate models:

Flipper length model: uses flipper length as the only predictor.

Body mass model: uses body mass as the only predictor.

Both models used the same training and testing sets. We standardized the predictor variables using StandardScaler within a pipeline. This ensures that the scaling parameters are learned from the training data only.


```{python}
# Model 1: Flipper length
flipper_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

flipper_model.fit(X_train_flipper, y_train)
```
```{python}
# Model 2: Body mass
mass_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

mass_model.fit(X_train_mass, y_train)
```
## Mondel Evaluation

# Result

# Discussion

The held-out test set results demonstrate that flipper length is a substantially stronger single predictor of Palmer penguin species than body mass, 
achieving an overall test accuracy of 0.837 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.715 compared to 0.744 accuracy and a 0.561 macro-averaged F1-score for body mass.
 This performance gap aligns with biological differences between structural skeletal traits and labile physiological traits in seabirds. 
 Once adult penguins reach maturity, flipper length remains relatively stable across the breeding season, providing a consistent morphological 
 signal across species. By contrast, body mass fluctuates considerably depending on recent foraging success, fasting during incubation, 
 and parental provisioning duties (Gorman et al., 2014), introducing within species variance that blurs decision boundaries in a single-predictor 
 logistic regression model.

Examining species-level errors reveals why overall accuracy remained below 0.85 for both single-feature classifiers. 
Gentoo penguins are noticeably larger in both flipper length and body mass than their congeners in the Palmer Archipelago, 
allowing both models to identify Gentoo individuals with high reliability. However, Adélie and Chinstrap penguins share very similar 
body mass distributions, causing the body mass classifier to misclassify nearly all test-set Chinstrap penguins as Adélie. 
While flipper length separated Adélie and Chinstrap penguins moderately better than body mass, a single linear boundary on one morphological 
feature cannot fully resolve overlapping measurements between these two smaller species.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, restricting each logistic regression model to a single predictor 
ignores complementary morphological traits—such as bill length and bill depth—that strongly distinguish Chinstrap penguins from Adélie penguins.
 Second, the dataset exhibits class imbalance across species and spans three breeding seasons across different islands in the Palmer Archipelago 
 (Horst et al., 2020), meaning environmental and inter-annual shifts in prey availability could influence body mass measurements. 
 Third, adult penguins exhibit sexual dimorphism in body size (Gorman et al., 2014), and pooling males and females without accounting for sex 
 increases overlap between smaller males of one species and larger females of another.

Future analyses could extend this work in three practical directions. First, fitting a multivariable logistic regression model or regularized 
classifier that combines flipper length with bill length and bill depth would quantify how much classification accuracy improves when structural 
bill morphology is included alongside flipper length. Second, incorporating penguin sex and nesting island as covariates or interaction terms could 
clarify whether accounting for sexual dimorphism resolves the remaining confusion between Adélie and Chinstrap penguins. Finally, evaluating non-linear 
classifiers such as random forests or support vector machines on the multi-feature dataset could test whether curved decision boundaries capture subtle 
morphological separation across all three species.
